svg.aria-label: Insulin and glucagon in glucose control: the secretion mechanism of the beta cell, glucose uptake through GLUT4 translocation, the difference in organ targets, the liver-only target of glucagon, and the asymmetry whereby several hormones raise glucose but only one lowers it.
svg.text: A How the beta cell senses glucose
glucose in through GLUT2
metabolised, ATP rises
ATP-sensitive K+ channel closes
cell depolarises, Ca2+ enters, insulin vesicles release
Incretins (GIP, GLP-1) amplify this, which is why oral glucose
releases more insulin than the same dose given intravenously.
B Insulin: the hormone of storage
Muscle and adipose
GLUT4 moved to the membrane: glucose uptake rises (the main effect)
Liver
glycogen synthesis up, breakdown down, new glucose production down
Adipose and whole body
lipid synthesis up, lipid breakdown down, protein synthesis up
C Glucagon: almost only the liver
glycogen broken down to glucose (fast)
new glucose made from amino acids and glycerol (sustained)
fatty acids oxidised to ketone bodies (long fast)
Only the liver has glucose-6-phosphatase, so only the liver can export free glucose.
D The asymmetry
Raise glucose: four hormones
glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, growth hormone
Lower glucose: insulin alone
Hypoglycaemia stops the brain within minutes and needs several layers of defence;
hyperglycaemia harms over years, so one hormone sufficed.
